I’ve gathered what I can from the sources available within the fetch/search limits. Below are verse-by-verse notes, with tradition-specific points where the sources provide them. Sources I couldn't reach (Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship monographs) are noted as gaps at the end.

---

## Overview of the Sin Offering (Leviticus 4)

The sin offering (Hebrew *ḥaṭṭāʾt*) is compulsory, not voluntary like the burnt, grain, and peace offerings of chapters 1–3. It deals with sins committed **unintentionally** — by inadvertence, error, or human frailty — not defiant "high-handed" rebellion (Numbers 15:30–31). The chapter classifies four categories of sinner: the anointed (high) priest (vv. 3–12), the whole congregation (vv. 13–21), a ruler (vv. 22–26), and a common person (vv. 27–35). The animal's value and the blood ritual vary by rank.

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1
**Then the LORD said to Moses** — A new section marker. The formula "Then the LORD spoke to Moses" occurs 23 times in Leviticus, each introducing fresh revelation. Whereas chapters 1–3 began with the voluntary formula "If any man of you bring," here the tone shifts to compulsory instruction dealing with sin. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm; Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/; Precept Austin / Rooker: https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_4_commentary)

### v. 2
**“If a person sins unintentionally…”** — The Hebrew *bišgāgâ* means "through inadvertence, want of consideration, straying." Gill explains it covers sins through ignorance of the law, forgetfulness, or error; the Jewish rabbis limited it to transgressions of *negative* commands that involve an *act* (not mere words or thoughts). (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

Guzik notes the Hebrew root for "sin" (*ḥāṭāʾ*) essentially means "to miss" — the same root used in Judges 20:16 for a slinger who does not miss. The contrast is between sins of human frailty and sins of outright rebellion. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

**Reformed / Ligonier:** Emphasizes that unintentional sins are not the same as "high-handed" sins (Num 15:22–31). A high-handed sin is committed boldly, defiantly, without remorse. Not all intentional sins are high-handed; David's adultery was intentional but he repented. The truly converted do not sin with a high hand. (Ligonier, search excerpt: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/sin-offering)

**Pulpit Commentary:** Even sins of inadvertence require expiation. Our Lord could say "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34) — even the crucifixion could be treated as a sin of ignorance, for which atonement was possible. (Pulpit via BibleHub: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/4-2.htm)

**Gill:** Notes Jewish tradition that the law's 613 commands include 248 affirmative and 365 negative; only negative transgressions require a sin offering here. Instances given: eating forbidden fat thinking it permitted; idolatry by bowing (thinking only sacrifice/incense was forbidden); Sabbath-breaking thinking it a common day. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm)

### v. 3
**“If the anointed priest sins, bringing guilt on the people…”** — "The anointed priest" (*hakkōhēn hammāšîaḥ*) means the high priest (Ellicott notes the phrase is unique to Leviticus). His sin brings corporate guilt — either because his example leads others astray, or because as representative head his guilt is imputed to the nation. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm)

**A young bull without blemish** — The same sacrifice as for the whole congregation (v. 14), showing the gravity of priestly sin. Guzik quotes Trapp: "The sins of teachers are the teachers of sins." (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

**Christological:** Gill notes the sin offering is called "sin" itself (the Hebrew word), and Christ is our antitype: 2 Cor 5:21 — "He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us." Guzik adds that Adam Clarke observed the LXX word for "sin offering" (*hamartia*) is the same word Paul uses. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm; Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

### v. 4
**“He must bring the bull…lay his hand on the bull’s head, and slaughter it…”** — The laying on of hands (repeated five times in this chapter: vv. 4, 15, 24, 29, 33) is central. **Spurgeon** identifies five meanings in the symbol: (1) confession of sin, (2) consent to substitution, (3) acceptance of the victim in the sinner's place, (4) belief in the transference of sin, (5) a dependence — a *leaning* on the victim. Spurgeon emphasizes the Hebrew implies leaning heavily, not a mere touch: "O my soul, lean hard on Christ, throw all the weight of thy sin upon him." (Guzik quoting Spurgeon: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/; Spurgeon sermon excerpts: https://www.biblehub.com/sermons/auth/spurgeon/the_sin-offering.htm)

**Gill:** Notes Targum Jonathan specifies the *right* hand. The killing could be done by a butcher, not necessarily the priest. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm)

### vv. 5–6
**Blood brought into the Tent of Meeting; sprinkled seven times before the veil.** — This is unique to the sin offerings for the priest and the congregation. The blood enters the Holy Place. **Seven** symbolizes completeness/perfection (Ellicott lists numerous biblical sevens: creation days, Day of Atonement sprinkling, Naaman's washing, Jericho, etc.). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

**Gill:** The priest dipped the finger of his *right* hand. Jewish canons required the right hand for blood manipulation. Whether the blood touched the veil itself or fell before it was debated; Jarchi said it was directed toward the veil but did not necessarily touch it. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm)

**Spurgeon:** The veil, made of costly tapestry, would by degrees "become more and more like a vesture dipped in blood" — picturing the blood of Christ that opens access to God. (Guzik quoting Spurgeon: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

**Guzik:** Sin offends God's holiness, so the veil guarding His presence must receive blood. Sin affects prayer, so the altar of incense must receive blood. Sin requires atonement, so the altar of burnt offering must receive blood. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

### v. 7
**Blood on the horns of the altar of incense; remainder poured at the base of the altar of burnt offering.** — The golden (incense) altar inside the Holy Place represents intercessory prayer. **Gill:** The blood on the horns shows that Christ's intercession proceeds on the basis of His blood (cf. Rev 8:3; 1 John 2:1). The pouring of the remainder at the bronze altar's base shows the efficacy of Christ's blood for atonement. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm)

**Ellicott:** According to Second Temple practice, the priest began at the northeast horn, proceeded northwest, southwest, southeast, dipping his finger afresh and wiping it between each horn. Two holes at the southwest horn of the altar drained blood into the Kidron brook. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

### vv. 8–10
**Removal and burning of the fat, kidneys, and lobe of the liver.** — Identical to the peace offering procedure (Lev 3:3–5). The choicest parts (fat = best) are offered to God. Gill notes the Jewish comment that just as the peace offering brings peace, so the sin offering restores peace after sin. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm)

### vv. 11–12
**The hide, flesh, head, legs, entrails, and dung burned outside the camp.** — Unlike other offerings where the skin went to the priest (Lev 7:8), the sin offering bull for priest or congregation was *not flayed*; it was cut in pieces and burned entirely — skin and all. This is burned at the ash heap outside the camp. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

**Christological significance:** Hebrews 13:11–12 applies this directly to Christ: "Jesus also suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through His own blood." The burning outside the camp signifies the shame and rejection Christ bore. **Guzik:** All selfish motives are removed — the offerer gains no meat or leather; the only motive is to be right with God. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

**Spurgeon:** The dung being burned depicts the reproach Christ endured. "See here a faint image of the fire which consumed the Saviour on Calvary!" The bodily pains were real, but "the sufferings of His soul must have been the very soul of His sufferings." (Spurgeon via BibleHub: https://www.biblehub.com/sermons/auth/spurgeon/the_sin-offering.htm)

### v. 13
**“If the whole congregation of Israel strays unintentionally…”** — The same Hebrew word for "unintentionally" (*bišgāgâ*) as v. 2. The phrase "the thing be hid from the eyes of the assembly" indicates corporate unawareness at the time of the act. According to later Jewish interpretation, "the whole congregation" refers to the Sanhedrin (the 71-member council) who through erroneous teaching could lead the nation into sin. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

An example of national inadvertent sin is 1 Samuel 14:32, where Israelites ate meat with blood after battle. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

### vv. 14–15
**The elders lay hands on the bull’s head** — This is the one difference from the priest's offering. The elders represent the whole nation; the congregation cannot all physically lay hands. In Second Temple practice, three members of the Sanhedrin performed this act. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

### vv. 16–21
**Procedure identical to vv. 5–12.** Blood sprinkled before the veil, applied to incense altar horns, remainder poured at bronze altar base. Fat burned on altar; rest burned outside camp. **v. 20** introduces the key promise: "the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven."

**Constable (via Precept Austin):** Notes the Hebrew root *kpr* (atonement) is understood by scholars in three ways: (1) "to cover" (Arabic cognate), (2) "to wipe/purge," (3) "to ransom." The latter two are preferred as going back to Hebrew rather than Arabic roots. Both purging and ransoming are valid contextually. (Constable excerpt: https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_4_commentary)

### v. 22
**“When a leader sins…”** — Hebrew *nāśîʾ*, "one lifted up." Gill says this may be a tribal chief or a king. Ellicott notes the exceptional phrase "the LORD *his God*" (absent in the other three cases), suggesting a king answerable only to God Himself. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

### vv. 23–26
**The ruler's offering: a male goat without blemish.** Notice the downgrade from a bull. The ritual is also simpler: blood does **not** enter the Holy Place; it is applied only to the horns of the *bronze altar* in the courtyard, with the remainder poured at its base. A common priest (not the high priest) officiates. The fat is burned on the altar, and the rest of the animal is available for the priest to eat (Lev 6:24–30). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm; Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

**Ellicott:** The Hebrew *śāʿîr* denotes the older, shaggy-haired he-goat, distinguished from the younger *ʿattûd* used for festival offerings. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

### vv. 27–31
**The common person's offering: a female goat (or lamb, vv. 32–35) without blemish.** Same courtyard ritual as the ruler's — blood on bronze altar horns, remainder poured at base, fat burned, priest eats the rest. The female animal reflects lesser cost, appropriate to ordinary means.

**Spurgeon:** "It is true the sins of great men cover a larger space, but yet there must be a bloody sacrifice for the smallest offenses. For the sins of a housewife or of a servant, of a peasant, or of a crossing-sweeper, there must be the same sacrifice as for the sins of the greatest and most influential." (Guzik quoting Spurgeon: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

**Meyer (via Guzik):** "It is very needful, then, for us to be perpetually cleansed in the precious blood of Christ. We must ask to be forgiven for the many sins which we know not, as well as for those we know." (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

**v. 31:** The phrase "a pleasing aroma to the LORD" appears here (and in v. 35) but is absent from the priest's, congregation's, and ruler's sin offerings. Ellicott suggests this indicates that the humblest gift of the humblest person, if sincerely offered, is as acceptable to God as the costliest offering. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)

### vv. 32–35
**Alternative: a female lamb.** The procedure is identical. The repetition reinforces that both goat and lamb are acceptable; the common person has a choice. Guzik notes this shows God's accommodation to varying economic circumstances without diminishing the seriousness of sin. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed (Ligonier)
- The sin offering is better understood as a **"purification offering."** It purified the sanctuary from the defilement caused by sin, not just the sinner. The blood cleanses the tabernacle so God can continue dwelling amid His people. (Ligonier search excerpt: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/sin-offering)
- Distinguishes between **"intentional sin" and "high-handed sin."** A converted person may commit intentional sin (as David did) but will feel contrition afterward, proving it was never high-handed. High-handed sin is the mark of the unconverted. (Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/sin-offering)

### Baptist (Spurgeon / desiringGod.org)
- **Spurgeon** emphasizes the *personal, weighty faith* in the substitute: the hand-laying is not a mere touch but a heavy leaning — "the very essence and nature of faith." The sin offering for the common person shows that Christ's atonement reaches the lowest. Spurgeon also stresses that sins of ignorance are still real sins needing real blood; our unknown sins were laid on Christ as surely as our known sins. (Spurgeon: https://www.biblehub.com/sermons/auth/spurgeon/the_sin-offering.htm)
- Spurgeon notes that under the New Covenant, even presumptuous sins are covered — something the Old Covenant sin offering could not address — but only through the same blood of Christ.

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
- Guzik reads the text with a strong **Christocentric typology** throughout, seeing Jesus in every detail: the unblemished bull (Christ's sinlessness), the hand-laying (imputation), the sevenfold sprinkling (perfect cleansing), the burning outside the camp (Christ's rejection). His application is pastoral and devotional, encouraging believers to keep short accounts with God over unintentional sins. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-4/)
- Notes that 1 John 1:9 provides atonement under the New Covenant for sins that under the Old Covenant had no sacrifice (presumptuous / high-handed sins).

### Evangelical (Precept Austin / Constable / MacDonald)
- **MacDonald:** The sin offering was for *redeemed people* — not a sinner coming for salvation, but an Israelite already in covenant seeking forgiveness. (MacDonald via Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_4_commentary)
- **Constable:** The sin offering is the principal *expiatory* offering, but textual evidence suggests the *burnt offering* was the principal atoning sacrifice; the sin offering's distinctive was *purification*. (Constable via Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_4_commentary)
- **Wenham** (cited at Precept Austin): Translates *ḥaṭṭāʾt* as "purification offering," arguing that all sacrifices atoned in some sense; the unique role of this one was cleansing the sanctuary. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_4_commentary)

---

## Other Views (from available sources)

### Modern Scholarship: "Purification Offering" vs. "Sin Offering"
Several scholars (Wenham, Milgrom, NET Bible notes) prefer the translation **"purification offering"** because the Hebrew *ḥaṭṭāʾt* primarily functioned to purge the sanctuary of ritual impurity, not merely to deal with the guilt of the sinner. The blood applied to sanctuary furniture cleansed the holy place from the contagion of sin. This view is noted at Precept Austin drawing on Wenham and the NET Bible notes. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_4_commentary)

### Older Commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit)
These consistently read the sin offering as typical of Christ's atonement. Gill in particular draws heavily on rabbinic sources (Maimonides, Jarchi, the Talmud) for procedural details — e.g., the exact age of animals, the order of horn-anointing, the right-hand rule for sprinkling. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/4.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/4.htm)
